title: He missed the rest
hook: if told someone speaks ill of you, say: he didn't know my other faults (Enchiridion 33)

segments.voice: Yesterday: your own deeds and dangers, which please you more than your listeners. Your line was ask, don't tell. What question did you ask, and what did you hear? Day three hundred sixty-eight.

A screenshot arrives with a short note above it: thought you should know. Someone has been saying things about you. It's easy to start drafting the reply right there in your head, point by point, with receipts and a closing line. Section thirty-three of the handbook has a one-line answer for this moment, far older than any screenshot. It's short, it's a little ridiculous, and it's a very good comeback. Today: he missed the rest.
screen: `THOUGHT YOU SHOULD KNOW.` → `ALREADY DRAFTING THE REPLY.` → `HE MISSED THE REST.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. If someone tells you that a certain person is speaking badly of you, Epictetus says, don't defend yourself against what was said. Instead, answer: he obviously didn't know my other faults, or he wouldn't have mentioned only these. Second, why it works. A defense keeps the argument alive. You go point by point, they answer, the circle grows. Epictetus' reply steps out of the contest entirely. It agrees, cheerfully, that you have faults, more than the critic knows, and so there's nothing left to fight about. The joke is on yourself, and nobody else gets hurt by it. Third, the Greek. The verb he uses for defend yourself belongs with apologia, a speech of defense, the word in the title of Plato's Apology, where Socrates defends himself at his trial. Epictetus' advice, roughly: skip the apologia. Fourth, what it isn't. It isn't self-hatred, and it isn't ignoring a fair point. If the critic is right about something, you've learned something. If they're wrong, nothing that belongs to you has been touched. We met that idea a couple of weeks ago, with the insult: it's not the words that harm you, but your judgment that you've been harmed. Today's line is that idea with a grin on its face. It costs nothing. And it ends the conversation better than any receipt.
screen: `DON'T DEFEND YOURSELF.` · `HE DIDN'T KNOW MY OTHER FAULTS.` · `SKIP THE APOLOGIA.` · `A FAIR POINT TEACHES; A WRONG ONE CAN'T HARM.` · then, large: `HE MISSED THE REST.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and breathe. Bring to mind one criticism that still stings, something said about you or to you, recently or long ago. Notice where it lands in your body. Notice the urge to argue with it. Now try Epictetus' answer, quietly, inside: he missed the rest. You might even smile. See if the sting changes. If part of the criticism was fair, let that part stay, and let the rest go. The bell holds the time.
He missed the rest. Epictetus' answer to someone speaking ill of you: they didn't know my other faults, or they'd have mentioned those too. Today's word.
Your line: he missed the rest. If a criticism reaches you today, answer it with humor instead of a defense, out loud or just inside. Day three hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes answer reported criticism with self-deprecating humor, as Epictetus suggests, rather than defending themselves point by point.

original.note: Greek: a speech of defense. Epictetus uses the related verb: don't defend yourself.

trapdoor: what you thought: ignore your critics.
what it means: don't defend; agree, with a smile, that you have even more faults than they named.
what a scholar hears: the verb is the one behind apologia, the defense speech of Plato's Apology, here set aside for a joke.
